target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good because it improves convenience, health, productivity, accessibility, and safety.
objection: Those benefits are often outweighed by harms: AI can replace workers and depress wages, weaken students’ and adults’ critical thinking by supplying easy answers, reproduce or intensify racial bias, and create major privacy and surveillance risks.

target: AG2’s argument that AI is not good for society because its harms in jobs, learning, bias, and privacy outweigh its benefits.
objection: Real risks do not prove AI is net harmful; AI can augment workers, support tutoring and verification in education, be audited for fairness, and be made more privacy-preserving through minimization, access controls, on-device processing, and differential privacy.

target: AG1’s claim that governance, audits, fairness testing, and privacy-preserving design can make AI good for society.
objection: Those fixes are too unreliable in practice because firms are incentivized toward speed and profit, oversight lags deployment, many systems are opaque, education guardrails are easy to ignore, and privacy techniques still leave meaningful risk.

target: AG2’s assumption that imperfect safeguards mean AI cannot be considered good for society.
objection: AI is not replacing a neutral baseline; human systems already have bias, privacy issues, and safety failures. AI can be monitored with audit trails, logging, and performance checks that are sometimes more measurable than human decision-making, so it can still improve outcomes relative to current methods.

target: AG1’s reliance on audit trails, monitoring, human review, and layered privacy controls as proof that AI can be managed safely.
objection: Audit trails do not guarantee accountability or understanding, AI can scale and accelerate human bias, human review can become rubber-stamping under volume, and privacy controls do not remove the underlying data-processing risks or power asymmetry.

target: AG2’s claim that safeguards such as audits, risk-tiering, tutor-style use, and privacy controls cannot work reliably.
objection: Harm can be reduced through staged deployment, feedback-driven correction, continuous telemetry, rollback, contestability, standardized reporting, and human review; not all AI use cases have the same risk profile, and the most beneficial uses like accessibility tools are lower risk and can be governed more tightly.

target: AG1’s claim that monitoring, rollback, human review, and lower-risk accessibility uses can make AI good for society.
objection: Monitoring often worsens privacy because it requires more data, rollback cannot undo harm already done, human review is often overwhelmed, and even lower-risk tools still depend on the same data-processing infrastructure that creates privacy and bias risks.

target: AG2’s claim that monitoring and oversight are inherently surveillance-heavy and ineffective.
objection: Monitoring can be privacy-preserving through aggregate metrics, short retention, access controls, and differential privacy; staged rollout and pre-deployment testing can prevent many failures before broad deployment; structured human review can avoid rubber-stamping; and accessibility tools still provide real societal benefit even when they process data.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving monitoring, testing, and structured oversight can solve the harms.
objection: Privacy-preserving monitoring reduces visibility and accountability, pre-deployment tests miss real-world edge cases, proprietary opacity makes oversight performative, and incentives still push companies toward the easiest path to deployment.

target: AG2’s claim that safeguards and oversight cannot be trusted because of incentives and opacity.
objection: Society can change incentives directly through procurement rules, mandatory independent evaluations, and liability for negligent deployment; independent behavioral audits can provide accountability even without full interpretability, and AI should be judged relative to current human baselines that are already biased and unsafe.

target: AG1’s claim that liability, audits, procurement rules, and risk-tiering can make AI net-good.
objection: Those mechanisms do not scale well across consumer apps, small businesses, and third-party integrations; audits are limited by vendor control and sampling; risk-classification can be gamed; and automated systems can still amplify bias, privacy invasion, and job displacement faster than governance can stop them.

target: AG2’s claim that governance is too weak to make AI good for society.
objection: AI benefits concentrate in lower-stakes uses like accessibility, health, and productivity, and governance does not need to be perfect to produce net gains. Concrete constraints such as privacy-by-design, limited retention, citations, and verification can improve outcomes over the human baseline.

target: AG1’s claim that lower-stakes AI can be kept separate from harmful uses and still be good for society.
objection: In real deployment, lower-stakes tools still create the same data and model infrastructure that feeds privacy and bias harms; spillover through shared systems and shared incentives is structural, and net benefits are not enough if the harms disproportionately fall on workers and racial minorities.

target: AG2’s claim that beneficial AI and harmful AI are inevitably entangled.
objection: Purpose limitation, data separation, compartmentalized pipelines, and enforceable impact-based testing can reduce spillover; accessibility and safety gains are real and should not be dismissed because higher-risk uses exist.

target: AG1’s claim that purpose limitation and compartmentalization can realistically stop spillover.
objection: Those controls are hard to enforce in centralized, multi-tenant systems; AI is integrated into analytics, ads, recommendation, and fraud systems; vendors have incentives to repurpose data; and impact testing only reveals harms after they have already occurred.

target: AG2’s claim that entanglement makes a broad restriction the safest choice.
objection: Not all AI use cases are equally risky, on-device and hybrid processing can reduce central entanglement, procurement and platform rules can govern integration points, and blanket restriction would sacrifice real accessibility and safety gains.

target: AG1’s claim that on-device and privacy-preserving architectures, combined with risk-tiering, can make low-risk AI beneficial.
objection: Even helpful AI creates centralized control, vendor lock-in, residual privacy risk, and incentive-driven classification problems; low-risk deployments can still normalize and entrench the broader harmful AI ecosystem.

target: AG2’s claim that centralized control and lock-in are unavoidable.
objection: Interoperability, portability, local/user-controlled modes, and accessibility-first standards can reduce lock-in and centralization, making AI governable rather than inherently harmful.

target: AG1’s portability, interoperability, and user-control proposals.
objection: Porting data does not port proprietary model behavior, user privacy settings are often cosmetic or overridden by defaults and updates, and accessibility-first standards do not solve spillover into labor displacement, surveillance, or learning harms.

target: AG2’s claim that portability and user controls cannot meaningfully constrain AI harms.
objection: Independent certification, continuous compliance, integration-level restrictions, separate model instances for different risk tiers, and outcome-based reporting can make controls real without banning AI; safety and accessibility can be protected by governing the supply chain and downstream use.

target: AG1’s certification, compliance, and integration-control proposals.
objection: Certification cannot keep up with rapid model updates and drift, audits certify paperwork rather than lived outcomes, incentives encourage strategic compliance, and even certified accessibility systems can still misrecognize accents, surveil users, and contribute to labor and learning harms.

target: AG2’s claim that operational safeguards cannot keep up with deployment reality.
objection: Operational safeguards can be tied to signed model versions, locked deployment pipelines, provenance tracking, contractual telemetry, meaningful liability, and stricter accessibility/education evaluation; these measures make governance practical rather than merely symbolic.

target: AG1’s operational safeguards and version-based compliance scheme.
objection: These safeguards increase surveillance because they require more logging and trace data, they do not scale across the broader market, liability only compensates after harm occurs, and education tools still tend to drift from scaffolding into answer-substitution under market incentives.

target: AG2’s conclusion that broad restriction is the safest default.
objection: Broad restriction would impose major opportunity costs by reducing disability supports, hazard detection, and learning assistance that help people now; instead, AI should be governed selectively through risk-tiering, with strong safeguards focused on high-stakes uses and preserved benefits in lower-risk domains.
